Remember, hand washing is one of the most effective ways to stay healthy, so let's make it a habit to wash our hands regularly.
summary: This lesson teaches Primary 1 pupils about the importance of hand washing in Nigeria. Pupils learn how to wash their hands properly, when to wash their hands, and why hand washing is crucial in our daily lives. The lesson includes examples, key points, activities, and fun facts to engage pupils and promote good hygiene practices. By the end of the lesson, pupils will understand the importance of hand washing and how to do it properly. The lesson also aims to promote good hygiene practices in Nigerian schools and communities, and to reduce the spread of illnesses.
learning_objectives: To understand the importance of hand washing in Nigeria
To learn how to wash hands properly
To identify the right times to wash hands
To promote good hygiene practices in Nigerian schools and communities
nigerian_examples: Chidi, a pupil in Abuja, washes his hands before eating a snack after playing football
Amina, who lives in Kano, washes her hands before cooking to prevent the spread of germs to the food
Tunde, a vendor in Lagos, uses hand sanitizer to clean his hands when he is not near a sink

subject: Physical & Health Education
content:
Introduction - Engage the child, explain why this topic matters in Nigerian daily life

Hello Primary 1 students, today we are going to learn about healthy foods. You know how sometimes your mom or dad takes you to the market in Lagos or Kano to buy food? Well, the food we eat is very important for our bodies. Just like a car needs fuel to move, our bodies need food to have energy to play, run and have fun. But not all foods are good for us, some foods can make us sick or weak. So, it's very important to eat healthy foods to stay strong and healthy. In Nigeria, we have a lot of delicious and healthy foods like jollof rice, egusi soup, and suya. Let's learn more about healthy foods and why they are important for our bodies.

Explanation - Thorough explanation of the concept in simple language a Primary 1 child understands

So, what are healthy foods? Healthy foods are foods that are good for our bodies. They give us energy, help us grow strong, and keep us from getting sick. Just like how you need to put the right kind of fuel in a car, we need to eat the right kind of food to keep our bodies working well. Healthy foods include fruits like apples, bananas, and oranges, vegetables like carrots, cabbage, and tomatoes, proteins like chicken, fish, and eggs, and whole grains like rice, bread, and pasta. We should try to eat a little bit of each of these foods every day to stay healthy. In Nigeria, we have a lot of healthy foods that are available and affordable. For example, you can buy a plate of akara and pap for 50 Naira, or a bunch of vegetables for 20 Naira.

Examples - At least 3 detailed Nigerian examples using Nigerian names, places, and Naira

Let's look at some examples of healthy foods in Nigeria. Chidi loves to eat akara and pap for breakfast. Akara is made from beans and is a good source of protein. Pap is made from corn and is a good source of carbohydrates. Chidi's mom buys the ingredients from the market in Abuja for 100 Naira. She then cooks them at home and serves them to Chidi and his siblings. Amina is another student who loves to eat fruits. She buys a basket of oranges from the market in Kano for 50 Naira. Oranges are a good source of vitamin C, which helps to keep us from getting sick. Tunde is a student who loves to eat suya. Suya is made from meat and is a good source of protein. Tunde's dad buys suya from a vendor in Lagos for 200 Naira. They then eat it together as a family. These are just a few examples of healthy foods that we can find in Nigeria. We should try to eat a variety of foods to stay healthy and strong.

Key Points - At least 5 bullet points summarising what was learned

Here are the key points we learned today:
* Healthy foods are foods that are good for our bodies
* We should eat a variety of foods to stay healthy and strong
* Fruits, vegetables, proteins, and whole grains are all examples of healthy foods
* We can find healthy foods in Nigeria, such as akara, pap, oranges, and suya
* We should try to eat healthy foods every day to stay healthy and strong

Activities - 2 fun hands-on activities a Nigerian child can do at home or school

Now, let's do some fun activities to help us remember what we learned today. Activity 1: Draw a picture of your favorite healthy food. What is your favorite food? Is it akara, pap, oranges, or suya? Draw a picture of it and write its name. Then, write why you like it and why it's good for your body. Activity 2: Create a healthy food plate. Imagine you are a chef in a restaurant in Abuja. You need to create a healthy food plate for your customers. What foods will you include on the plate? Will you include fruits, vegetables, proteins, and whole grains? Draw a picture of the plate and write the names of the foods you included. Then, write why you chose those foods and why they are good for the body.

Fun Facts - 2 interesting facts related to the topic in a Nigerian context

Here are two fun facts about healthy foods in Nigeria. Fact 1: Did you know that Nigeria is one of the largest producers of yams in the world? Yams are a good source of carbohydrates and are very healthy for our bodies. We can boil them, fry them, or roast them. Fact 2: Did you know that the Nigerian government has a program to promote healthy eating in schools? The program is called the School Feeding Program and it provides free meals to students in public schools. The meals are made with healthy ingredients and are designed to help students stay healthy and focused in school.
summary: In this lesson, Primary 1 students learned about healthy foods and why they are important for our bodies. They learned about different types of healthy foods, such as fruits, vegetables, proteins, and whole grains, and how they can find them in Nigeria. They also did fun activities to help them remember what they learned, such as drawing pictures of their favorite healthy foods and creating healthy food plates. By the end of the lesson, students knew the importance of eating healthy foods every day to stay healthy and strong.
learning_objectives: To understand the concept of healthy foods and their importance for our bodies
To identify different types of healthy foods, such as fruits, vegetables, proteins, and whole grains
To recognize the availability of healthy foods in Nigeria and their affordability
To develop healthy eating habits and make informed choices about the foods they eat
nigerian_examples: Chidi loves to eat akara and pap for breakfast, which are made from beans and corn and are good sources of protein and carbohydrates
Amina buys a basket of oranges from the market in Kano for 50 Naira, which are a good source of vitamin C
Tunde's dad buys suya from a vendor in Lagos for 200 Naira, which is made from meat and is a good source of protein

subject: Physical & Health Education
content:
Introduction

Hello Primary 1 pupils, today we are going to learn about Playground Safety. Do you like playing with your friends in the school playground or at home? I'm sure you do. Playing is an important part of our daily life, and it helps us to stay healthy and strong. However, it's also important to know how to play safely so that we don't get hurt. In Nigeria, many children like to play football, basketball, and other games in the playground. But sometimes, they may trip and fall or collide with their friends. That's why we need to learn about playground safety.

Explanation

So, what is playground safety? Playground safety means being careful and following rules when we play in the playground. It's like following traffic rules when we are on the road. Just as we need to stop at the zebra crossing and look left and right before crossing the road, we also need to follow rules when we play in the playground. For example, we should always check the playground equipment before we use it, and we should never push or shove our friends when we are playing.

Playground safety is important because it helps us to prevent injuries. Imagine if you are playing on the swings and you fall off because the swing is broken. You might get hurt, and you might even need to go to the hospital. But if you had checked the swing before you got on, you would have seen that it was broken and you wouldn't have gotten hurt. That's why it's so important to be careful and follow the rules when we play in the playground.

Examples

Let's look at some examples of playground safety in Nigeria. Chidi is a pupil in Lagos, and he loves playing football with his friends in the school playground. One day, while they were playing, Chidi saw that the goal post was broken. He immediately told his friends to stop playing and went to tell the teacher. The teacher was very proud of Chidi for being so careful and responsible. She fixed the goal post, and then the children could continue playing safely.

Amina is another pupil who loves playing on the slides in the playground. One day, she saw that the slide was slippery because it had rained the night before. She decided to wait until the sun came out and dried the slide before she played on it. Her friends were very proud of her for being so careful, and they all waited together until it was safe to play.

Tunde is a pupil in Abuja, and he loves playing basketball with his friends. One day, while they were playing, Tunde saw that one of the hoops was broken. He immediately stopped the game and told his friends to wait while he went to tell the teacher. The teacher was very happy with Tunde for being so responsible, and she fixed the hoop so that the children could continue playing safely.

In Kano, there is a big playground where children love to play. The playground has a big sign that says, 'Please check the equipment before you use it.' The children in Kano are very careful and always follow the rules. They check the equipment before they use it, and they never push or shove each other when they are playing. As a result, they rarely get hurt, and they have a lot of fun playing together.

Imagine you are in a playground in Lagos, and you see a big sign that says, 'Please do not play on the broken swings.' What would you do? You would probably tell your friends to stay away from the broken swings and find something else to play on. That's the right thing to do. If you see something that is broken or not safe, you should always tell a grown-up so that they can fix it.

Key Points

Here are some key points to remember about playground safety:

* Always check the playground equipment before you use it.

* Never push or shove your friends when you are playing.

* Always tell a grown-up if you see something that is broken or not safe.

* Be careful when you are playing on the swings, slides, and other equipment.

* Always follow the rules and listen to the teacher or other grown-ups in charge.

Activities

Now, let's do some fun activities to help us remember what we have learned. Activity 1: Draw a picture of your favorite playground equipment, and write a sentence about how to use it safely. For example, if you draw a picture of a swing, you could write, 'Always check the swing before you get on, and hold on tight when you are swinging.' Activity 2: Role-play a scenario where you are playing in the playground and you see something that is broken or not safe. What would you do? How would you tell your friends to stay away from it? Practice what you would say and do in a situation like this.

Fun Facts

Here are some fun facts about playground safety in Nigeria. Did you know that many schools in Nigeria have special playground monitors who help to keep the children safe during playtime? These monitors make sure that the equipment is safe and that the children are following the rules. Did you know that the Nigerian government has special rules to help keep children safe in playgrounds? For example, all playgrounds must have soft surfaces like sand or grass to help prevent injuries if a child falls.

Now, let's review what we have learned today. We learned that playground safety is very important, and that we need to always check the equipment before we use it. We also learned that we should never push or shove our friends when we are playing, and that we should always follow the rules and listen to the teacher or other grown-ups in charge. And finally, we learned that if we see something that is broken or not safe, we should always tell a grown-up so that they can fix it.
summary: This lesson teaches Primary 1 pupils about playground safety, including the importance of checking equipment before use, not pushing or shoving friends, and following rules. The lesson includes examples from Nigerian schools and playgrounds, and provides activities and fun facts to reinforce learning. By the end of the lesson, pupils will be able to identify safe and unsafe behaviors in the playground and take steps to prevent injuries. The lesson aligns with the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council (NERDC) curriculum for Physical and Health Education. The expected outcome of this lesson is that pupils will demonstrate an understanding of playground safety rules and procedures, and will be able to apply these rules in a practical setting. The lesson will help pupils to develop essential life skills, including the ability to identify and manage risks, and to take responsibility for their own safety and the safety of others.
learning_objectives: To understand the importance of playground safety
To identify safe and unsafe behaviors in the playground
To learn how to prevent injuries in the playground
To develop essential life skills, including risk management and responsibility for personal safety
nigerian_examples: Chidi, a pupil in Lagos, saw that the goal post was broken and immediately told his friends to stop playing and went to tell the teacher.
Amina, a pupil, saw that the slide was slippery and decided to wait until the sun came out and dried the slide before she played on it.
Tunde, a pupil in Abuja, saw that one of the hoops was broken and immediately stopped the game and told his friends to wait while he went to tell the teacher.

subject: Physical & Health Education
content:
Introduction

Hello pupils, today we are going to learn about running and jumping. These are very important physical activities that we use every day in Nigeria. Do you know why we need to learn about running and jumping? It is because they help us to stay healthy and strong. Just like Chidi, who lives in Lagos, and loves to play football with his friends during recess. They run around and jump to kick the ball, and it makes them happy and healthy. Running and jumping are also important skills that we use in our daily lives, like when we are playing games, or running to catch a bus in Abuja, or jumping over obstacles in Kano. So, let's learn more about running and jumping and how we can use them to stay healthy and have fun.

Explanation

So, what is running? Running is when we move our legs very fast to get from one place to another. We use our feet to push the ground and make ourselves move forward. Just like Amina, who lives in Kano, and loves to run to school every morning. She says it helps her to wake up and feel fresh for the day. Running is very good exercise for our bodies, it helps to make our hearts strong and our legs fast. And what is jumping? Jumping is when we use our legs to push ourselves up into the air. We use our muscles to lift ourselves up and then we come back down to the ground. Just like Tunde, who lives in Abuja, and loves to jump over hurdles during sports day. He says it makes him feel like a superhero.

Examples

Let's look at some examples of running and jumping in Nigerian daily life. For instance, imagine you are at the National Stadium in Lagos, and you are watching a football match between Nigeria and Ghana. The players are running around the field, trying to kick the ball into the goal. They are using their running skills to get ahead of the other team and score a goal. Or, imagine you are at a school sports day in Kano, and you are participating in a jumping competition. You are trying to jump over a hurdle that is 50 Naira coins high. You use your jumping skills to clear the hurdle and win a prize. Another example is, imagine you are at a market in Abuja, and you are running to catch a bus that is about to leave. You use your running skills to get to the bus on time, and you pay the bus fare of 100 Naira to get to your destination.

Key Points

Here are some key points to remember about running and jumping:

* Running is a great way to stay healthy and strong
* Jumping is a fun way to challenge ourselves and get exercise
* We use our legs to push ourselves forward when we run
* We use our muscles to lift ourselves up when we jump
* Running and jumping are important skills that we use in our daily lives

Activities

Now, let's do some fun activities to practice our running and jumping skills. Activity 1: Running Relay. Divide into teams and line up at one end of the field. The first person in each team runs to the other end of the field, then runs back to their team and tags the next person. The next person then runs to the other end of the field and back, and so on. The team that finishes first wins. Activity 2: Jumping Contest. Set up a series of hurdles or obstacles, such as small cones or books, and see who can jump over them the fastest. You can time each person and keep track of who is the fastest jumper.

Fun Facts

Here are some fun facts about running and jumping in Nigeria. Did you know that the fastest runner in Nigeria is Blessing Okagbare, who won a gold medal in the 100 meters at the African Championships? She is from Delta State and is known for her speedy runs. Another fun fact is that the highest jumper in Nigeria is Mike Edwards, who jumped 2.2 meters high at the National Sports Festival in Abuja. He is from Lagos State and is known for his impressive jumping skills.
summary: This lesson teaches Primary 1 pupils about running and jumping, two important physical activities that help us stay healthy and strong. Pupils learn about the benefits of running and jumping, and how to use these skills in their daily lives. The lesson includes fun activities, such as a running relay and a jumping contest, to help pupils practice their skills. By the end of the lesson, pupils will understand the importance of running and jumping and how to use these skills to stay healthy and have fun.
learning_objectives: To understand the importance of running and jumping in everyday life
To learn how to run and jump safely and effectively
To develop an appreciation for physical activity and exercise
To build confidence and self-esteem through physical activity
nigerian_examples: Chidi, who lives in Lagos, and loves to play football with his friends during recess
Amina, who lives in Kano, and loves to run to school every morning
Tunde, who lives in Abuja, and loves to jump over hurdles during sports day

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content:
**Introduction**
Hello, children! Today we are going to learn about something very important - Being a Good Citizen. A citizen is someone who belongs to a country, and a good citizen is someone who helps make their community and country a better place for everyone.

**Explanation**
As Nigerians, we are all citizens of Nigeria. Being a good citizen means following rules, respecting others, helping our community, and taking care of things we share with other people, like schools, parks, and streets.

Good citizens follow rules and laws, even small ones - like waiting your turn in line, not littering, and obeying traffic rules. Good citizens are honest and respect other people's property and feelings. Good citizens also help their community - this could mean helping to keep your school clean, being kind to classmates, or helping a neighbour in need.

Good citizens also take care of public property, like school desks, books, playground equipment, and public toilets - things that belong to everyone, not just one person. When everyone takes care of shared things, the whole community benefits.

Even children can be good citizens! Every small good action - like picking up litter, sharing with a friend, or telling the truth - helps make Nigeria a better place.

**Examples**
1. In her school in Port Harcourt, Ngozi always picks up rubbish she sees on the ground, even if it's not hers, and puts it in the bin to keep the school compound clean.

2. In Abuja, when Daniel found a wallet on the ground, he gave it to his teacher instead of keeping it, so it could be returned to its owner.

3. At a community event in Jos, a group of children helped sweep the local football field before a match so everyone could play on a clean, safe ground.

**Key Points**
- A citizen is someone who belongs to a country.
- A good citizen follows rules, respects others, and helps their community.
- Good citizens are honest and take care of shared property.
- Even small actions, like picking up litter, make a difference.
- Children can be good citizens too!

**Activities**
1. Make a list of 3 things you can do this week to be a good citizen at home or school - for example, throwing rubbish in the bin or helping a friend.
2. Role-play a situation where you find something that belongs to someone else. Practice what a good citizen would do.

**Fun Facts**
1. In Nigeria, citizens can vote for their leaders once they turn 18 years old - this is one important way adult citizens participate in their country.
2. Many Nigerian schools have 'environmental clubs' where students work together to keep their school compounds clean and plant trees - a great example of good citizenship in action!
summary: This lesson teaches children that being a good citizen means following rules, respecting others, being honest, and helping take care of their community - and that even small actions by children can make a positive difference.
learning_objectives: Understand what it means to be a citizen and a good citizen
Identify behaviours that show good citizenship, like honesty and following rules
Recognize the importance of taking care of shared/public property
Apply good citizenship in everyday actions at home and school
nigerian_examples: Ngozi picking up rubbish to keep her school compound clean in Port Harcourt
Daniel returning a found wallet to his teacher in Abuja instead of keeping it
Children sweeping a community football field before a match in Jos

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content:
**Introduction**
Hello, children! Have you ever wondered who helps fix things when they break, who helps when someone is sick, or who keeps us safe? Today we will learn about Community Helpers - the wonderful people who work to make our communities better places to live!

**Explanation**
A community helper is someone whose job helps other people in the community. Community helpers do many different jobs, but they all share one thing in common - their work helps make life better, safer, or easier for everyone around them.

Some community helpers work to keep us healthy, like doctors and nurses who treat sick people in hospitals. Some keep us safe, like police officers who help when there is trouble, and firefighters who put out fires. Some help us learn, like teachers in our schools. Others help our community run smoothly, like market traders who sell food, drivers who take people places, and refuse collectors who keep our streets clean.

Every community helper deserves our respect and thanks because their work benefits all of us, even when we don't always notice it.

**Examples**
1. Nurse Funmilayo works at a health centre in Ibadan. Every day, she helps mothers bring healthy babies into the world and treats children who are sick with malaria.

2. Officer Musa is a policeman in Kaduna. He helps direct traffic at busy junctions so that cars and people can cross safely, and he helps find lost children.

3. Mr. Okafor drives a danfo bus in Lagos every day, helping hundreds of people get to work, school, and the market on time.

**Key Points**
- Community helpers are people whose jobs help others in the community.
- Doctors and nurses keep us healthy.
- Police officers and firefighters keep us safe.
- Teachers help us learn.
- We should respect and thank community helpers for their work.

**Activities**
1. Think of three community helpers you have seen in your area. Draw a picture of one of them doing their job.
2. Role-play with a friend or family member - take turns pretending to be a community helper (like a doctor, teacher, or police officer) and act out how they help people.

**Fun Facts**
1. In many Nigerian markets, there are special helpers called 'load carriers' or 'truck pushers' who help traders move heavy goods - an important community job!
2. Community health workers in rural Nigerian villages often travel by bicycle or motorbike to reach families who live far from hospitals, bringing important health care to them.
summary: This lesson introduces children to community helpers - the people whose jobs benefit everyone in the community, including doctors, police officers, teachers, and market traders - and encourages children to appreciate and respect their work.
learning_objectives: Understand what a community helper is
Identify different types of community helpers and their roles
Recognize how community helpers benefit everyone
Develop respect and appreciation for community helpers
nigerian_examples: Nurse Funmilayo helping mothers and treating sick children at a health centre in Ibadan
Officer Musa directing traffic and helping find lost children in Kaduna
Mr. Okafor driving a danfo bus to help people get around Lagos

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content:
**Introduction**
Good morning, children! Today we are going to talk about something very special - our families. A family is a group of people who love and take care of each other. Every family is different, and every family is special in its own way!

**Explanation**
A family can include your mother, father, brothers, sisters, grandparents, aunties, uncles, and cousins. Some families are big with many people living together, and some families are small. Some children live with both parents, some live with one parent, and some live with grandparents or other relatives who love and care for them. All of these are families!

In a family, everyone has a role to play. Parents and guardians take care of the children, provide food, clothing, and send children to school. Children can help too - by being respectful, helping with small chores, and being kind to brothers and sisters.

Families also teach us important things like our culture, our language, good manners, and how to treat other people. This is why family is so important in our lives.

**Examples**
1. Tunde lives with his mother, father, younger sister Bisi, and his grandmother in Ibadan. Every evening, the whole family eats dinner together and talks about their day.

2. Amaka lives with her aunty in Owerri because her parents work in another city. Her aunty takes care of her just like a mother would, helping with homework and cooking her favourite foods.

3. In Kano, Yusuf's family includes his parents, four siblings, and his grandparents who all live in the same compound. Everyone helps each other - the older children help younger ones with reading, and grandparents tell stories in the evening.

**Key Points**
- A family is a group of people who love and care for each other.
- Families come in different sizes and shapes - big, small, with parents, grandparents, or guardians.
- Everyone in a family has a role to play.
- Families teach us culture, language, and good manners.
- We should respect and appreciate our families.

**Activities**
1. Draw a picture of your family members. Write or say the name of each person and how they are related to you.
2. Think of one helpful thing you can do for your family this week, like helping to set the table or tidying your room. Tell your family about your plan!

**Fun Facts**
1. In Nigeria, many families are 'extended families', meaning grandparents, aunties, uncles, and cousins often live close together or even in the same house.
2. In many Nigerian cultures, children are taught to greet elders with respect, such as kneeling or bowing slightly, as a sign of love and honour for family members.
summary: This lesson teaches children that families come in many different forms - big or small, with parents, guardians, or extended relatives - and that every family member has a role in showing love, care, and support for one another.
learning_objectives: Understand what makes up a family
Recognize that families come in different forms and sizes
Identify the roles different family members play
Appreciate the importance of family in teaching culture and values
nigerian_examples: Tunde's family in Ibadan eating dinner together every evening
Amaka being cared for by her aunty in Owerri while her parents work away
Yusuf's extended family living together in Kano, helping each other every day

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content:
**Introduction**
Good day, children! Nigeria is a big country with many different people, and each group of people has its own special way of life. This way of life is called 'culture'. Today we will learn about Our Culture and why it makes Nigeria such a colourful and exciting place!

**Explanation**
Culture means the way a group of people lives - including their language, food, clothes, music, dance, festivals, and traditions. Nigeria has over 250 different ethnic groups, and each one has its own unique culture! Some of the largest groups include the Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, and many others, but there are also many smaller groups, each with beautiful traditions.

Culture is passed down from parents and grandparents to children through stories, songs, festivals, and everyday life. For example, different groups have their own traditional clothing - like the Yoruba aso-oke, the Hausa babban riga, and the Igbo isiagu. Different groups also have their own foods, like jollof rice, pounded yam with egusi soup, tuwo shinkafa, and many more delicious dishes!

Learning about our culture - and the cultures of other Nigerians - helps us understand and respect each other, and it makes us proud of who we are.

**Examples**
1. During the Yoruba 'Eyo' festival in Lagos, people dress in colourful costumes and parade through the streets, celebrating their culture with music and dance.

2. In Igbo communities, the 'New Yam Festival' is celebrated every year to give thanks for a good harvest, with feasting, dancing, and traditional ceremonies.

3. In Hausa culture, the Durbar festival features beautifully decorated horses and riders parading through towns during special celebrations like Eid.

**Key Points**
- Culture is the way a group of people lives - their language, food, clothes, music, and traditions.
- Nigeria has over 250 ethnic groups, each with its own unique culture.
- Culture is passed down from parents and grandparents to children.
- Different groups have different traditional clothing and foods.
- We should respect and celebrate the cultures of all Nigerians.

**Activities**
1. Ask a parent or grandparent to teach you a traditional song, dance, or story from your culture. Practice it and share it with your class or family.
2. Draw a picture of a traditional outfit from your culture (or any Nigerian culture you know about) and colour it with bright colours.

**Fun Facts**
1. Nigeria has over 500 languages spoken across the country - one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world!
2. Many Nigerian festivals, like the Argungu Fishing Festival in Kebbi State, bring together thousands of people for fishing competitions, music, and celebration.
summary: This lesson introduces children to the concept of culture - the language, food, clothing, music, and traditions of different groups of people - and highlights Nigeria's rich cultural diversity, encouraging children to value and celebrate all Nigerian cultures.
learning_objectives: Recognize that Nigeria has many different ethnic groups and cultures
Identify examples of cultural traditions like festivals, clothing, and food
Develop respect and pride for Nigerian cultures
nigerian_examples: The Yoruba 'Eyo' festival in Lagos with colourful costumes and parades
The Igbo 'New Yam Festival' celebrating a good harvest with feasting and dancing
The Hausa Durbar festival with decorated horses parading during Eid celebrations

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content:
**Introduction**
Hello, children! Roads are everywhere - in our towns, near our schools, and in front of our homes. But roads can also be dangerous if we don't know how to use them safely. Today we will learn about Road Safety so that we can stay safe whenever we are near roads.

**Explanation**
Road safety means knowing the rules and habits that keep us safe when walking, crossing, or travelling on roads. Cars, buses, motorcycles (often called okada), and trucks move very fast, and a person who is not careful can get hurt.

Here are some important road safety rules: Always look left and right before crossing a road, even if it looks empty. Use a pedestrian crossing (zebra crossing) if there is one nearby. Hold an adult's hand when crossing the road if you are young. Never run across a road - always walk. Wear a seatbelt when riding in a car, and wear a helmet when riding on a motorcycle. Always cross at a safe place, not from between parked cars where drivers cannot see you.

Traffic lights and signs also help keep us safe. A red light means stop, green means go, and yellow means get ready. Learning these rules and following them every time helps prevent accidents.

**Examples**
1. Before crossing the busy road near her school in Lagos, Halima always stops, looks left, looks right, and looks left again before crossing carefully with her teacher.

2. In Enugu, Chukwuemeka's father always makes sure everyone wears a seatbelt before starting the car, even for short trips to the market.

3. At a busy junction in Kano, a traffic warden uses hand signals and a whistle to help cars and pedestrians move safely, just like a traffic light would.

**Key Points**
- Always look left and right before crossing a road.
- Use pedestrian crossings when available.
- Hold an adult's hand when crossing as a young child.
- Never run across roads - always walk carefully.
- Wear seatbelts in cars and helmets on motorcycles.

**Activities**
1. Practice the 'Stop, Look, Listen' routine with an adult - stand at the edge of a safe spot, stop, look both ways, listen for vehicles, then decide if it's safe to cross.
2. Draw a picture of a traffic light and colour each light correctly: red, yellow, and green. Write what each colour means.

**Fun Facts**
1. In Nigeria, traffic wardens called 'LASTMA' in Lagos and other state traffic agencies help manage traffic and keep roads safe for everyone.
2. The zebra crossing got its name because the black and white stripes painted on the road look like the stripes on a zebra!
summary: This lesson teaches children important road safety rules, including looking both ways before crossing, using pedestrian crossings, holding an adult's hand, and wearing seatbelts and helmets, to help keep them safe near roads and traffic.
learning_objectives: Understand why road safety is important
Learn the 'look left, look right' rule before crossing roads
Recognize the meaning of traffic light colours
Identify safe practices like wearing seatbelts and helmets
nigerian_examples: Halima safely crossing a busy road near her school in Lagos with her teacher
Chukwuemeka's father ensuring everyone wears a seatbelt in Enugu
A traffic warden using hand signals to manage traffic at a busy junction in Kano

subject: Teamwork
content: When your team finishes something hard, celebrate together! Celebrating means saying 'good job' to each other, high-fiving, or feeling proud together. Celebrating makes everyone feel happy and want to work together again.
summary: Celebrate team successes together! Say 'good job', give high-fives, and feel proud. Celebrating builds happiness and strengthens teams.
learning_objectives: Learn why celebrating team success matters
Understand how celebration builds team bonds
nigerian_examples: Nigerian football teams celebrate goals together as a team
After school competitions, Nigerian students cheer for their classmates
Families celebrate children's achievements with praise and encouragement

subject: Teamwork
content: Every person in a team has a job to do. Doing your part means finishing your job so the team can succeed. If one person doesn't do their job, the whole team struggles. Be someone your teammates can count on!
summary: Every team member has a job. Doing your part means finishing your job. If one person fails, the whole team struggles. Be reliable!
learning_objectives: Learn why each role matters in a team
Develop reliability as a team member
nigerian_examples: In Nigerian relay races, every runner must do their part to win
School group projects fail if one student doesn't do their assigned work
Each family member doing chores makes the home run smoothly

subject: Teamwork
content: In a team, everyone's ideas matter. When you listen to your teammates, you learn new ideas and make everyone feel important. Good listeners help teams make better decisions together. Always give your teammates a chance to speak.
summary: Everyone's ideas matter in a team. Listening helps you learn new ideas and makes teammates feel important. Good listeners help teams make better decisions.
learning_objectives: Learn why listening to teammates is important
Understand how listening improves team decisions
nigerian_examples: In Nigerian football teams, players listen to their captain's instructions
During school debates, team members listen before responding
Family meetings in Nigeria require everyone to listen to each other

subject: Teamwork
content: Sharing is very important in a team. When you share supplies, ideas, and turns, everyone can do their part. Sharing shows you care about the team's goal more than just yourself. Great teams share everything!
summary: Sharing supplies, ideas, and turns helps everyone do their part. Sharing shows you care about the team's goal. Great teams share everything!
learning_objectives: Understand why sharing matters in teams
Learn what to share in a team
See how sharing builds team success
nigerian_examples: Sharing pencils and erasers during Nigerian exams shows teamwork
During Nigerian group projects, sharing ideas creates better results
Taking turns with playground equipment shows good team sharing

subject: Teamwork
content: Teamwork means working together to get something done. When you work as a team, everyone helps. A team can be friends, family, or classmates. Together, you can do things that are hard to do alone.
summary: Teamwork means working together. Everyone helps. Teams can be friends, family, or classmates. Together you can do hard things.
nigerian_examples: Nigerian football teams win by working together, not just one player
Families work as a team to prepare for festivals like Eid and Christmas
Classroom cleaning in Nigerian schools requires teamwork

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: Computers have programs that let you draw and paint. A common drawing program is Paint (on Windows computers). You can use the mouse to draw lines, shapes, and pictures. Tools include: pencil (draws thin lines), brush (draws thick lines), eraser (removes mistakes), fill bucket (fills areas with color), and shape tools (draw circles, squares, triangles). You can also use a drawing tablet if available. Drawing on computer is different from drawing on paper because you can undo mistakes and try again without wasting paper. Have fun creating digital art!
summary: Computer drawing programs have tools: pencil, brush, eraser, fill bucket, shapes. You can undo mistakes. Drawing on computer saves paper.
learning_objectives: Understand how digital drawing differs from paper
nigerian_examples: Nigerian children drawing the Nigerian flag on a computer
Creating birthday cards using Paint
Drawing animals and sharing with classmates

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: Educational games are computer or tablet games that help you learn while having fun. They can teach math, reading, spelling, science, and other subjects. Examples include math games where you solve problems to earn points, spelling games where you type missing letters, and puzzle games that build thinking skills. Educational games are different from regular games because learning is the main goal. Ask your teacher or parents to recommend good educational games. Set a time limit so you balance playing with other activities like reading and outdoor play.
summary: Educational games help you learn math, reading, spelling, and more while having fun. Ask adults for recommendations. Balance game time with other activities.
nigerian_examples: Math games used in Nigerian computer labs
Spelling apps recommended by teachers
Educational games on tablets during breaks

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: The internet is a network that connects computers all over the world. It lets you find information, watch videos, play games, and talk to people far away. To use the internet, you need a device (computer, tablet, phone) and an internet connection (Wi-Fi or mobile data). A browser is a program that lets you visit websites. Examples: Chrome, Firefox, Safari. To go to a website, type its address in the bar at the top. The internet is a wonderful tool, but always use it with an adult's permission and supervision.
summary: The internet connects computers worldwide. You need a device and connection. Browsers like Chrome let you visit websites. Always use with adult supervision.
learning_objectives: Practice safe internet use with adults
nigerian_examples: Using the internet to learn about Nigerian history
Watching educational videos on YouTube with parent supervision
Accessing online learning platforms from home

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: The keyboard is how you type letters, numbers, and symbols into a computer. The middle row of letters is called the home row: A, S, D, F, G, H, J, K, L. Your fingers should rest on these keys. Your left hand goes on A, S, D, F. Your right hand goes on J, K, L. Your thumbs rest on the spacebar. Practice typing with all fingers, not just one or two. The shift key makes capital letters. The enter key starts a new line. The more you practice, the faster you will type!
summary: Keyboard has home row keys: A,S,D,F (left hand) and J,K,L (right hand). Thumbs on spacebar. Shift key for capitals. Enter key for new line.
learning_objectives: Learn proper finger placement on home row
nigerian_examples: Nigerian students typing on computers in school labs
Learning to type your name and address
Practicing typing on a laptop at home

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: A password is a secret word or number that keeps your account safe. Never share your password with anyone except your parents. A good password is hard to guess. Do not use your name, birthday, or simple words like 'password' or '12345'. Use a mix of letters, numbers, and symbols. For example, 'Blue2Fish!' is a strong password. Change your password sometimes to keep it secure. If you think someone knows your password, tell a parent right away so they can help you change it.
summary: Passwords keep accounts safe. Never share passwords except with parents. Use strong passwords with letters, numbers, symbols. Change passwords sometimes.
learning_objectives: Learn how to create strong passwords
nigerian_examples: Using a password to protect your tablet at home
Creating a password for educational apps
Asking parent before sharing any password

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Air is all around us even though we cannot see it. We breathe air to live. Wind is moving air. When air moves slowly, it feels like a gentle breeze. When air moves fast, it feels like strong wind. Wind can be helpful: it dries clothes, blows seeds to grow new plants, and cools us on hot days. Wind can also be powerful: strong winds can blow down trees or roofs during storms. You can feel air when you wave your hand or blow on your skin.
summary: Air is invisible but all around us. Wind is moving air. Gentle wind is a breeze. Strong wind can be powerful. We breathe air to live.
learning_objectives: Understand that air exists even though invisible
Describe helpful and powerful effects of wind
nigerian_examples: Flying kites during harmattan winds
Wind drying laundry in Nigerian compounds
Wind turbines in some Nigerian states producing electricity

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Simple machines are tools that make work easier. They help us lift, move, or cut things with less effort. Some simple machines are: lever (see-saw, bottle opener), pulley (flag pole, well bucket), wheel and axle (bicycle, car), inclined plane (ramp, slide), wedge (knife, axe), and screw (lid on a bottle). Simple machines are everywhere around us. When you use a see-saw at the playground, you are using a lever. When you ride a bicycle, you use wheels and axles.
summary: Simple machines make work easier: lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw. They help us lift, move, and cut things.
learning_objectives: Understand how simple machines help us
Find examples of simple machines in daily life
nigerian_examples: Using a bottle opener (lever) to open soft drinks
Pulling water from a well using a pulley
Riding a bicycle (wheel and axle) in the neighborhood

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Soil is the loose top layer of the earth where plants grow. Soil is made of tiny pieces of rock, dead leaves, and animal remains. There are different types of soil: sandy soil (feels rough, drains water fast), clay soil (feels sticky, holds water), and loamy soil (best for farming). Farmers need good soil to grow crops like yam, cassava, maize, and vegetables. Soil also provides homes for animals like earthworms, ants, and beetles.
summary: Soil is where plants grow. Types: sandy (rough), clay (sticky), loamy (best for farming). Soil gives us food and homes for animals.
learning_objectives: Identify what soil is made of
Understand why soil is important for farming
nigerian_examples: Yam farming in loamy soil in Benue State
Clay soil used for pottery in Abuja
Earthworms found in Nigerian garden soil

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Your body has five special senses that help you understand the world around you. Sight (eyes) lets you see colors, shapes, and movements. Hearing (ears) lets you listen to sounds like music, voices, and birds. Touch (skin) lets you feel if something is hot, cold, soft, or hard. Taste (tongue) lets you enjoy sweet, sour, salty, and bitter foods. Smell (nose) lets you enjoy nice smells like food and flowers, and avoid bad smells. Your senses work together to keep you safe and happy every day!
summary: Five senses: sight (eyes), hearing (ears), touch (skin), taste (tongue), smell (nose). Senses help you understand and stay safe in the world.
learning_objectives: Identify the five senses and their body parts
Explain how senses keep us safe
nigerian_examples: Using sight to read Nigerian road signs
Using smell to enjoy jollof rice cooking
Using touch to feel the texture of ankara fabric

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Weather is what the air outside is like each day. In Nigeria, we have two main seasons: the dry season and the rainy season. The dry season has hot sun, little rain, and dusty winds called harmattan. The rainy season has lots of rain, cooler temperatures, and thunderstorms. Each season affects what we wear, what we eat, and what we do. During the rainy season, we wear raincoats and carry umbrellas. During the dry season, we drink more water and wear lighter clothes.
summary: Nigeria has two seasons: dry season (hot, little rain) and rainy season (lots of rain). Weather affects our clothes, food, and activities.
learning_objectives: Understand how seasons affect daily life
nigerian_examples: Harmattan dust from the Sahara during dry season
Heavy rains that fill rivers in Lagos and Port Harcourt
Farmers planting crops at the start of rainy season

subject: Communication
content: Asking questions is how you learn new things. When you do not understand something, ask! Good questions start with words like who, what, where, when, why, and how. For example: 'Who wrote this book?' 'What time is lunch?' 'Why is the sky blue?' Raise your hand in class before asking. Be polite: say 'Excuse me' or 'May I ask a question?' There is no such thing as a silly question — if you are wondering, others probably are too. Asking questions shows you are curious and want to learn.
summary: Asking questions helps you learn. Use who, what, where, when, why, how. Raise your hand. Say 'Excuse me.' No question is silly.
learning_objectives: Learn how to ask good questions
Understand question words (who, what, where, when, why, how)
nigerian_examples: Asking a teacher 'Please can you explain that again?'
Asking a parent 'What is for dinner tonight?'
Asking a friend 'Where did you buy that book?'

subject: Communication
content: Expressing feelings means telling others how you feel inside. You might feel happy, sad, angry, scared, excited, worried, or loved. Use words to describe your feelings. Say 'I feel happy because...' or 'I feel sad when...' It is okay to have all kinds of feelings. When you are angry, take a deep breath before speaking. Say 'I feel angry because...' instead of shouting. Sharing your feelings helps others understand you. It also helps you feel better when you are upset. Your feelings are important and valid.
summary: Express feelings with words: 'I feel happy/sad/angry/excited because...' Take a breath before speaking when angry. Sharing feelings helps others understand you.
learning_objectives: Understand that all feelings are valid
nigerian_examples: Telling a parent 'I feel sad that my friend moved away'
Saying 'I feel excited about the school trip'
Sharing 'I feel proud that I passed my test'

subject: Communication
content: Group discussions are when a few people talk together about a topic. In a discussion, everyone gets a turn to speak. Listen when others talk. Do not interrupt. When it is your turn, share your idea clearly. You can agree with someone by saying 'I agree because...' You can disagree politely by saying 'I see it differently because...' Ask questions to understand others better. Group discussions help you learn from different perspectives. They also help you practice speaking and listening with others.
summary: In group discussions: take turns, don't interrupt, listen to others. Agree politely: 'I agree because...' Disagree politely: 'I see it differently...'
learning_objectives: Learn to agree and disagree politely
nigerian_examples: Discussing a class project in small groups
Talking about what to do for Children's Day celebration
Sharing ideas about a story the class read together

subject: Communication
content: Polite words show respect and kindness to others. Always use 'please' when asking for something. Say 'thank you' when someone helps you or gives you something. Say 'sorry' or 'I apologize' when you make a mistake. Say 'excuse me' when you need to get past someone or interrupt politely. Say 'you're welcome' when someone thanks you. Using polite words makes people feel good. It also makes them want to help you again. Polite words cost nothing but mean everything. Make them a habit every day!
summary: Polite words: please, thank you, sorry, excuse me, you're welcome. They show respect and kindness. Use them every day. They cost nothing but mean everything.
learning_objectives: Learn key polite words and phrases
Know when to use each polite word
nigerian_examples: Saying 'please may I have water?' at home
Saying 'thank you' to the school cleaner
Saying 's' when you accidentally bump someone

subject: Communication
content: Telling stories is a wonderful way to share experiences and ideas. A good story has a beginning, middle, and end. The beginning introduces the characters and setting. The middle tells what happened (the problem or adventure). The end tells how things turned out. Use words like 'first,' 'next,' 'then,' and 'finally' to help your listener follow along. Speak clearly and use expression in your voice. You can tell stories about things that happened to you, stories you made up, or folk tales you heard. Practice telling stories to family and friends!
summary: Good stories have beginning, middle, end. Use first, next, then, finally. Speak clearly with expression. Tell real or made-up stories.
nigerian_examples: Telling a story about your trip to visit grandparents
Sharing what happened at school during dinner
Retelling a Nigerian folk tale you heard

subject: Confidence Building
content: Asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness. Everyone needs help sometimes — even teachers and parents! When you are stuck on a problem, don't know what to do, or feel confused, ask for help. You can ask a parent, teacher, older sibling, or friend. Say politely, 'Can you help me, please?' Tell them what you need help with. After they help, say 'Thank you.' Asking for help shows that you want to learn and get better. Confident people know when to ask for help.
summary: Asking for help is strength, not weakness. Ask parents, teachers, or friends politely. Say what you need. Say thank you. Confident people ask for help.
learning_objectives: Understand that asking for help is good
Learn how to ask for help politely
nigerian_examples: Asking a teacher to explain a math problem again
Asking a friend to help find a lost item
Asking a parent for help with homework

subject: Confidence Building
content: Everyone feels afraid sometimes. Fear is normal. But you can learn to face your fears and become braver. First, name your fear. Say, 'I am afraid of speaking in class.' Next, take small steps. If you fear speaking, practice at home first. Then speak in front of one friend. Then try in class. Remember that mistakes are okay — everyone makes them. Breathe deeply when you feel scared. Tell yourself, 'I can do this.' Every time you face a fear, you get braver and more confident.
summary: Facing fears builds bravery. Name your fear, take small steps, practice. Breathe deeply, say 'I can do this.' Mistakes are okay.
nigerian_examples: Afraid of speaking in class? Practice answering at home first
Afraid of making friends? Smile and say hello to one person
Afraid of swimming? Start by putting your feet in the water

subject: Confidence Building
content: Self-talk is what you say to yourself in your head. Positive self-talk means saying kind, encouraging things to yourself. Instead of thinking 'I can't do this,' say 'I will try my best.' Instead of 'I'm not good at math,' say 'I am getting better at math every day.' Positive self-talk makes you feel strong and confident. Negative self-talk makes you feel sad and weak. Listen to the words in your head. If they are mean, change them to kind words. You are your own best cheerleader!
summary: Positive self-talk means saying kind words to yourself. Instead of 'I can't,' say 'I will try.' You are your own best cheerleader.
learning_objectives: Learn to replace negative thoughts with positive ones
nigerian_examples: Before a test, say 'I studied hard and I will do well'
Before a sports game, say 'I am strong and ready'
When something is hard, say 'I can learn this step by step'

subject: Confidence Building
content: Praising effort means celebrating how hard someone tried, not just the result. When you try your best, be proud of yourself even if you didn't win. Say to yourself, 'I worked really hard on this.' Praise your friends when they try hard, even if they make mistakes. Praising effort teaches that trying is what matters most. When you focus on effort, you are not afraid of making mistakes. You keep trying until you succeed. Every time you try hard, you are growing your brain and your confidence.
summary: Praise effort, not just results. Be proud when you try hard. Praise friends for trying. Effort helps you learn and grow. Trying matters most.
learning_objectives: Learn to praise yourself and others for trying
Build growth mindset through effort focus
nigerian_examples: Praising a friend who tried their best in a spelling bee, even if they didn't win
Being proud of yourself for studying hard, even with a fair grade
Encouraging a sibling who is learning a new skill

subject: Confidence Building
content: Setting small goals helps you build confidence. A goal is something you want to achieve. Small goals are easy to reach, like reading one book, learning five new words, or tying your shoes by yourself. When you reach a small goal, you feel proud and want to try bigger goals. Write down your goals or tell them to a parent. Celebrate when you finish a goal. Every time you reach a goal, your confidence grows. Start with easy goals first, then try harder ones as you get better.
summary: Small goals build confidence. Examples: read a book, learn five words, tie shoes. Reach goals, feel proud, then try bigger goals.
learning_objectives: Learn to set achievable small goals
nigerian_examples: Goal: Learn to spell your full name correctly
Goal: Finish homework before dinner for one week
Goal: Help with one chore at home every day

subject: Creativity
content: Craft making is using your hands and imagination to create things. You can make crafts from paper, cardboard, cloth, beads, or recycled materials. Examples: paper animals, greeting cards, jewelry from beads, or models from cardboard boxes. Craft making helps you practice cutting, gluing, folding, and painting. Don't worry if your craft doesn't look perfect — your creation is special because you made it. Use safe scissors and ask an adult for help if needed. Display your crafts at home or give them as gifts to make others smile.
summary: Craft making uses hands and imagination. Use paper, cardboard, beads, recycled items. Practice cutting, gluing, folding. Your creation is special because you made it.
nigerian_examples: Making paper beads from old magazines
Creating cards for Eid or Christmas
Building a model house from cardboard

subject: Creativity
content: Patterns are designs that repeat. You can create patterns with shapes, lines, and colors. Examples: stripes (straight lines repeated), zigzags (up and down lines), dots (repeated circles), and checkerboards (squares of two colors). Nigerian fabrics like Ankara have beautiful patterns. You can draw patterns on paper, in your notebook, or on cards. Patterns help you practice drawing carefully and spotting repetition. Start with simple patterns, then try more complex ones. Pattern drawing is relaxing and creative.
summary: Patterns repeat: stripes, zigzags, dots, checkerboards. Nigerian fabrics have beautiful patterns. Start simple, then try complex.
nigerian_examples: Drawing patterns inspired by Ankara fabric
Creating stripe patterns on a card
Making a checkerboard pattern with two colors

subject: Creativity
content: Inventing games means creating your own rules and activities. You can make up a new game with friends using things you have. First, decide the goal: How do you win? Next, make rules: What can players do? What can't they do? Then, try the game. If something isn't fun, change the rules. You can invent games with a ball, a rope, or just running. You can invent indoor games like board games or card games. Inventing games helps you think creatively, solve problems, and have fun with friends.
summary: Invent games: decide goal and rules. Try it, then improve rules. Use a ball, rope, or nothing. Inventing games builds creativity and problem-solving.
nigerian_examples: Inventing a new street game with friends
Creating a ball game with different scoring rules
Making up a rain game to play indoors

subject: Creativity
content: Singing and dancing are creative ways to express yourself. You can sing songs you know or make up your own. You can dance freely or learn dance steps. Nigerian music has many rhythms — try moving your body to the beat. Singing helps you remember things like the alphabet song. Dancing keeps your body healthy and strong. You don't need to be perfect — just have fun! Sing with family, at school, or in a choir. Dance at celebrations, parties, or just because you feel happy.
summary: Singing and dancing express yourself. Sing known songs or make up your own. Dance to Nigerian rhythms. Have fun and be creative.
learning_objectives: Explore singing and dancing as creative expression
nigerian_examples: Singing Nigerian children's songs
Dancing to Afrobeats music
Performing at school cultural day

subject: Creativity
content: Storytelling is creating and sharing stories. You can make up characters, places, and adventures. Start with 'Once upon a time...' or 'One day...' Give your characters names and personalities. Describe where the story happens — a forest, a city, or a magical land. Make a problem happen, then solve it at the end. Use your voice to make it exciting — speak loudly for giants, softly for mice. Tell stories to family, friends, or classmates. Every time you tell a story, you become a better storyteller.
summary: Storytelling: create characters, places, adventures. Start with 'Once upon a time.' Describe setting. Create a problem, then solve it. Use your voice.
learning_objectives: Learn story elements (characters, setting, problem, solution)
nigerian_examples: Creating a story about a clever tortoise
Telling a story about a child's adventure in Lagos
Making up a tale about animals in the forest

subject: CRS / Islamic Studies
content: The Five Pillars of Islam are the five most important acts of worship for Muslims. Shahada is believing there is only one God and Muhammad is His prophet. Salah is praying five times a day facing Mecca. Zakat is giving charity to help people in need. Sawm is fasting during the month of Ramadan. Hajj is making a pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime if able. These pillars help Muslims grow closer to God and be good people. Learning about the pillars helps you understand Islamic faith and practice.
summary: Five Pillars of Islam: Shahada (belief), Salah (prayer), Zakat (charity), Sawm (fasting), Hajj (pilgrimage). They help Muslims worship God and help others.
learning_objectives: Learn the names of the Five Pillars
Appreciate the importance of worship and charity
nigerian_examples: Nigerian Muslims praying Salah at the mosque near their home
Families giving Zakat to poor neighbors during Ramadan
Children learning to fast for half-days during Ramadan

subject: CRS / Islamic Studies
content: Honesty means telling the truth and not lying or stealing. Forgiveness means choosing not to be angry at someone who hurt you and giving them another chance. Both honesty and forgiveness are very important in Christianity and Islam. The Bible says, 'Do not lie to one another.' The Quran says, 'God loves those who are truthful.' When you make a mistake, say you are sorry and ask for forgiveness. When someone says sorry to you, forgive them just as you want God to forgive you.
summary: Honesty is telling the truth. Forgiveness is letting go of anger and giving second chances. Both are valued in Christianity and Islam. Say sorry and forgive others.
nigerian_examples: Telling your teacher the truth even if you might be in trouble
Forgiving a friend who broke your toy after they say sorry
Admitting when you took something that wasn't yours

subject: CRS / Islamic Studies
content: Abraham was a prophet respected by Christians and Muslims. He believed in one God and taught people to worship only God. Abraham was known for his great faith and obedience. He left his home because God asked him to go to a new land. Abraham showed kindness to strangers and welcomed guests. He is called the 'Friend of God' in the Bible and a great prophet in the Quran. Children can learn from Abraham to trust God, be kind to others, and follow what is right even when it's hard.
summary: Abraham was a prophet who believed in one God. He showed faith, obedience, and kindness. Christians and Muslims both respect Abraham as a great example.
learning_objectives: Apply Abraham's good qualities in daily life
nigerian_examples: Nigerian Christian children learning about Abraham in Sunday school
Muslim children hearing about Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) during Islamic lessons
Families showing hospitality to guests like Abraham did

subject: CRS / Islamic Studies
content: Love means caring deeply for others and wanting what is best for them. Service means helping others without expecting anything in return. Jesus taught his followers to 'love your neighbor as yourself'. In Islam, helping others is a form of worship. You can show love and service by helping your parents at home, sharing with friends, visiting sick relatives, or helping a younger child with schoolwork. Small acts of kindness every day show love and service. When you help others, you make the world a better place.
summary: Love is caring for others. Service is helping without expecting return. Help parents, share with friends, visit the sick. Small kindnesses make a big difference.
nigerian_examples: Helping your mother with chores after school
Sharing your lunch with a friend who forgot theirs
Visiting a grandparent who is feeling unwell

subject: CRS / Islamic Studies
content: Worship means showing love, honor, and thanks to God. Prayer is one way to worship. Christians pray to God through Jesus. Muslims pray Salah five times a day facing Mecca. Both Christians and Muslims believe prayer helps you talk to God, say thank you, ask for help, and say sorry for mistakes. You can pray anywhere — at home, at school, or outside. Prayer can be spoken out loud or silent in your heart. Regular prayer helps you feel close to God and remember to be a good person every day.
summary: Worship is showing love to God. Prayer is talking to God. Christians and Muslims both pray. You can pray anywhere, anytime. Prayer brings you closer to God.
learning_objectives: Learn about prayer in Christianity and Islam
nigerian_examples: Christian families praying before meals in Nigerian homes
Muslim children learning to pray Salah at the mosque
School morning assemblies with prayer

subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
content: Drama is a story acted out by people on a stage. Acting means pretending to be someone else. Nigerian drama includes traditional masquerade performances, village theatre, and modern Nollywood movies. Nollywood is Nigeria's movie industry, which is the second largest in the world after Hollywood. Actors and actresses in Nollywood tell Nigerian stories about family, love, and culture. Drama helps people understand different points of view, express feelings, and entertain others. You can do drama at school by acting out stories or playing pretend with friends.
summary: Drama is acting out stories. Nollywood is Nigeria's movie industry, the world's second largest. Acting helps express feelings and tell Nigerian stories.
learning_objectives: Understand what drama and acting are
nigerian_examples: Nollywood movies watched in homes across Nigeria and Africa
School drama clubs performing plays
Traditional masquerade performances in villages

subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
content: Folk tales are traditional stories passed down from grandparents to children. Many Nigerian folk tales teach lessons about honesty, kindness, and wisdom. A popular folk tale character is Tortoise, who is clever but often greedy and gets into trouble. Other animal characters include the hare, elephant, lion, and spider. Folk tales were traditionally told in the evening under the moonlight (called 'moonlight tales'). Grandparents would tell stories while children listened, learned, and sometimes sang along. Folk tales help preserve culture and teach good behavior.
summary: Folk tales are traditional stories that teach lessons. Tortoise is a common character who is clever but greedy. Moonlight tales are told in the evening.
learning_objectives: Learn about common folk tale characters
nigerian_examples: Tortoise and the birds story teaching not to be greedy
Why the tortoise has a cracked shell
Moonlight storytelling sessions in villages

subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
content: Music is an important part of Nigerian culture. Different ethnic groups have different musical instruments and styles. Yoruba music features talking drums (dùndún), bata drums, and shekere (a gourd with beads). Igbo music uses ogene (metal gong), ekwe (slit drum), and ubo (thumb piano). Hausa music features kalangu (talking drum), kakaki (long trumpet), and garaya (lute). Modern Nigerian music includes Afrobeats, made famous by artists like Fela Kuti and now Burna Boy, Wizkid, and Davido. Music is used for celebrations, ceremonies, storytelling, and entertainment.
summary: Nigerian music includes traditional instruments: talking drums (Yoruba), ogene (Igbo), kalangu (Hausa). Modern Afrobeats is famous worldwide.
learning_objectives: Appreciate music's role in Nigerian culture
nigerian_examples: Talking drums used at Yoruba weddings and festivals
Ogene played during Igbo ceremonies
Listening to Afrobeats at parties and on the radio

subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
content: Pottery is the art of making objects from clay. Clay is soft, wet dirt that can be shaped. After shaping, the clay is baked in a hot oven called a kiln. The baking makes the clay hard and strong. In Nigeria, pottery has been made for thousands of years. The Yoruba make pots for cooking and storing water. The Igbo make decorated pots for ceremonies. The Hausa make large pots for storing grains. Pottery is used for cooking, eating, storing food and water, and decoration. You can try simple pottery with modeling clay at school.
summary: Pottery makes objects from clay. Clay is shaped, then baked in a kiln to harden. Nigerian pottery is used for cooking, storing water, and ceremonies.
nigerian_examples: Yoruba water pots kept in homes
Igbo ceremonial pots with decorative patterns
Hausa grain storage pots (zana)

subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
content: Weaving is making fabric by crossing threads together on a loom. In Nigeria, weaving is an ancient craft. The Yoruba weave Aso Oke fabric for special occasions like weddings and festivals. The Hausa weave traditional caps (hula) and blankets. The Igbo weave baskets from palm leaves. Other crafts include pottery (making pots from clay), beadwork (stringing beads to make jewelry), and carving (shaping wood into masks or statues). Crafts are made by hand and show the creativity of Nigerian artists. You can try simple weaving with paper or string at home.
summary: Weaving makes fabric on a loom. Nigerian weaves: Aso Oke (Yoruba), hula caps (Hausa), baskets (Igbo). Other crafts: pottery, beadwork, carving.
nigerian_examples: Aso Oke fabric worn at Yoruba weddings
Hausa embroidered caps (hula) worn by n
Igbo baskets used for carrying produce

subject: English Studies
content: Nouns and verbs are two important types of words. A noun is a person, place, animal, or thing. Examples of nouns: teacher (person), school (place), dog (animal), book (thing). A verb is an action word — it tells what someone or something does. Examples of verbs: run, jump, eat, sleep, read, write. Every complete sentence needs at least one noun and one verb. For example: 'The cat (noun) sleeps (verb).' 'My mother (noun) cooks (verb).' Learning nouns and verbs helps you build good sentences!
summary: Nouns are people, places, animals, or things. Verbs are action words (run, jump, eat). Every sentence needs at least one noun and one verb.
learning_objectives: Understand that sentences need both nouns and verbs
nigerian_examples: The word 'Lagos' is a noun (place). 'Olu' is a noun (person).
In 'Children play football,' 'children' is a noun and 'play' is a verb.
In 'The trader sells yams,' 'trader' and 'yams' are nouns, 'sells' is a verb.

subject: English Studies
content: Reading short stories helps you learn new words and understand how sentences work. When you read a story, look at the pictures, sound out new words, and think about what is happening. After reading, ask yourself: Who was in the story? Where did it happen? What happened first, next, and last? Reading a little bit every day makes you a better reader. Start with stories that have big letters and colorful pictures. As you get better, you can read longer stories!
summary: Reading short stories builds vocabulary. Look at pictures, sound out new words. Ask: Who? Where? What happened? Read a little every day to improve.
learning_objectives: Practice reading short stories with comprehension
Learn to identify characters, setting, and plot
nigerian_examples: Nigerian children's books like 'Chidi's New Home' are great for Grade 2 readers
School libraries in Lagos and Abuja have short story collections for young readers
Teachers read Nigerian folk tales aloud while students follow along

subject: English Studies
content: A simple sentence is a group of words that tells a complete thought. Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a period (.), question mark (?), or exclamation point (!). A simple sentence has one noun and one verb. Examples: 'The bird sings.' 'I like rice.' 'She runs fast.' 'We play together.' You can make a sentence longer by adding describing words: 'The big bird sings loudly.' But even a short sentence like 'Go!' can be a sentence if it has a verb and a complete thought.
summary: A simple sentence is a complete thought. It starts with a capital letter and ends with . ? or ! Every sentence needs at least one verb and usually a noun.
learning_objectives: Identify what makes a complete sentence
Write simple sentences with capital letters and correct punctuation
Distinguish between complete sentences and sentence fragments
nigerian_examples: I love jollof rice. (complete sentence)
The bus to Abuja leaves at 7am. (complete sentence)
Playing football after school. (not a complete sentence — missing who plays)

subject: English Studies
content: Spelling means writing words correctly using the right letters in the right order. Some common words you use every day are: 'the', 'and', 'to', 'of', 'for', 'with', 'you', 'are', 'have', 'said'. A good way to learn spelling is to say the word slowly, write it down, check it, and try again. Practilling words like 'friend' (f-r-i-e-n-d), 'because' (b-e-c-a-u-s-e), and 'beautiful' (b-e-a-u-t-i-f-u-l). The more you read and write, the better your spelling becomes!
summary: Spelling means writing words with the right letters in the right order. Learn common words: the, and, to, for, you, are, have, said. Practice makes perfect.
learning_objectives: Learn to spell common Grade 2 words
Practice spelling strategies (say it, write it, check it)
Build spelling confidence through regular practice
nigerian_examples: Nigerian spelling bees help children practice common words
Teachers give weekly spelling tests in Nigerian primary schools
Writing words like 'Lagos', 'Benin', and 'Kano' helps with geography and spelling

subject: English Studies
content: The English alphabet has 26 letters. These letters are divided into two groups: vowels and consonants. Vowels are the letters A, E, I, O, U (and sometimes Y). Consonants are all the other letters like B, C, D, F, and so on. Every word in English must have at least one vowel sound. Try saying the vowels: A (ah), E (eh), I (ee), O (oh), U (oo). Vowels let your breath flow freely from your mouth. Consonants block the air in different ways using your lips, tongue, or teeth. Understanding vowels and consonants helps you spell and pronounce words correctly!
summary: Vowels: A, E, I, O, U. Consonants: all other 21 letters. Every word needs at least one vowel. Vowels let air flow freely; consonants block the air.
learning_objectives: Identify the 5 vowel letters in English
Understand that every word needs a vowel
nigerian_examples: The word 'LAGOS' has vowels A and O, consonants L, G, S
The word 'ABUJA' has vowels A, U, A and consonants B, J
In Nigerian classrooms, students sing vowel songs to remember A, E, I, O, U

subject: Hygiene Development
content: Hair care means keeping your hair clean, healthy, and neat. Wash your hair with shampoo at least once a week. Rinse out all the shampoo. After washing, dry your hair with a clean towel. Brush or comb your hair every day to remove tangles. Different hair types need different care. Ask your parents how to care for your hair type. If you have braids or cornrows, keep them neat. Do not share combs or brushes with others because germs can spread. Healthy hair looks shiny and feels soft.
summary: Hair care: wash weekly with shampoo, rinse well, dry, brush daily. Don't share combs. Healthy hair is shiny and soft.
learning_objectives: Learn proper hair washing and brushing
Understand why not to share hair tools
nigerian_examples: Washing hair on weekends before school week starts
Getting braids or cornrows done neatly
Using a personal comb or brush labeled with your name

subject: Hygiene Development
content: Healthy habits are things you do every day to keep your body strong and well. They include washing hands before eating, brushing teeth twice a day, bathing daily, getting enough sleep, drinking water, and eating fruits and vegetables. Healthy habits prevent sickness and help you grow. Make a routine: wake up, brush teeth, wash face, eat breakfast, go to school. After school: wash hands, eat, play, do homework, bathe, brush teeth, sleep. Small habits every day keep you healthy and ready to learn and play.
summary: Healthy habits: wash hands, brush teeth, bathe, sleep enough, drink water, eat fruits and vegetables. Daily routine keeps you strong.
nigerian_examples: Drinking water from a clean bottle during school break
Eating oranges or bananas as snacks instead of sweets
Going to bed early to wake up fresh for school

subject: Hygiene Development
content: Nail care means keeping your fingernails and toenails clean and healthy. Dirt and germs can hide under long nails and make you sick. Use nail clippers to cut your nails straight across. Cut them every 1-2 weeks. Wash under your nails when you wash your hands. Do not bite your nails. Keep a nail brush by the sink to clean under nails. Healthy nails are smooth and pink. If your nails change color or hurt, tell a parent.
summary: Nail care: cut nails every 1-2 weeks with clippers. Don't bite nails. Wash under nails. Healthy nails are smooth and pink.
learning_objectives: Avoid bad habits like nail biting
nigerian_examples: Using nail clippers bought from the market
Keeping a nail brush near the bathroom sink
Asking parents to help cut nails safely

subject: Hygiene Development
content: Personal grooming means taking care of how you look and feel. It includes brushing your hair, keeping your nails clean and short, and wearing clean clothes. Brush your hair every morning to keep it tidy. Cut your fingernails and toenails regularly so dirt doesn't collect under them. Use a comb or brush that is clean. Grooming helps you look neat and feel confident. When you look good, you feel good! Good grooming also shows respect for yourself and others around you.
