Home workout videos
Dance fitness classes
School physical education

subject: Physical & Health Education
content: Injury prevention means taking steps to avoid getting hurt during physical activity. Key strategies: warm up before exercise (5-10 minutes light activity like jogging, dynamic stretches), cool down after exercise (light activity + static stretches), use proper equipment (sports shoes, shin guards, helmets, knee pads), follow rules (no dangerous play), stay hydrated (drink water before, during, after), listen to your body (stop if you feel pain), build strength gradually (don't do too much too soon). Common injuries: sprains (stretched ligaments), strains (pulled muscles), fractures (broken bones), concussions (brain injury). In Nigerian schools, warm-ups before sports day prevent injuries. RICE treatment for minor injuries: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.
summary: Injury prevention: warm up, cool down, proper equipment, follow rules, hydrate, listen to body, gradual training. RICE for minor injuries: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.
nigerian_examples: Football players wearing shin guards during matches
Dynamic stretches before inter-house sports
Cyclists wearing helmets on Nigerian roads

subject: Physical & Health Education
content: Mental health includes emotional, psychological, social well-being. Affects thinking, feeling, acting. Common conditions: anxiety (excessive worry), depression (persistent sadness, loss of interest), eating disorders, ADHD (attention difficulty), bipolar disorder, schizophrenia. Causes: genetics, brain chemistry, trauma, environment, stress. Warning signs: mood changes, social withdrawal, extreme feelings, sleep/appetite changes, substance use, thoughts of self-harm. Help: talk to trusted adult, therapist, counselor, doctor; call helplines. Nigerian mental health: Nigerian Mental Health Association, Mentally Aware Nigeria Initiative. Reduce stigma by speaking openly, educating others. Self-care: sleep, exercise, healthy food, stress management, hobbies, connection. Mental health equals physical health.
summary: Mental health = emotional, psychological, social well-being. Common conditions: anxiety, depression, ADHD. Seek help from trusted adults, professionals. Reduce stigma.
nigerian_examples: Nigerian Mental Health Association
Mentally Aware Nigeria Initiative
School counselors
Helplines

subject: Physical & Health Education
content: Sports medicine prevents, diagnoses, treats sports injuries. Professionals: athletic trainers, physical therapists, sports doctors. Common injuries: sprains (ligaments), strains (muscles), fractures (bones), concussions (brain), shin splints, ACL tears. Treatment: RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation), physical therapy, surgery for severe cases, rehabilitation. Prevention: proper warm-up/cool-down, strength training, flexibility, equipment, technique, rest days. Nigerian sports medicine: football clubs have medical teams, Olympic athletes receive care. Student athletes: listen to body, report pain, follow rehab protocols, don't rush return. Sports medicine also covers nutrition (performance), psychology (resilience), biomechanics (efficient movement).
summary: Sports medicine prevents/treats injuries. Professionals: athletic trainers, physical therapists, doctors. Common injuries: sprains, strains, fractures, concussions. Prevention: warm-up, strength, equipment, rest.
nigerian_examples: Football club medical teams
Olympic athlete care
School sports first aid
Rehab programs

subject: Physical & Health Education
content: Sports psychology is the study of how mindset affects athletic performance. Key concepts: goal setting (SMART goals - Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound), visualization (imagining successful performance), self-talk (positive internal dialogue), concentration (focusing on task, ignoring distractions), arousal control (managing nervousness), and resilience (bouncing back from failure). Nigerian athletes like Blessing Okagbare use sports psychology to prepare for competitions. Before a match, visualize success: 'I see myself scoring the winning goal.' Use positive self-talk: 'I am strong, I am prepared, I can do this.' Sports psychology works for any performance: exams, presentations, music recitals.
summary: Sports psychology: mindset affects performance. Tools: SMART goals, visualization, positive self-talk, concentration, resilience. Used by Nigerian athletes. Works for exams and presentations too.
nigerian_examples: Nigerian footballers visualizing penalty kicks before matches

Student visualizing successful exam performance

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: Constitutional democracy means government based on a written constitution that limits power and protects citizens' rights. Nigeria's 1999 Constitution is the supreme law. Features: separation of powers among Executive, Legislative, Judicial; federalism (shared power between national and state governments); fundamental rights (freedom of speech, religion, assembly); regular elections; rule of law (no one above law). Democratic principles include consent of governed, majority rule with minority rights, accountability, transparency, checks and balances. Nigerian democracy faces challenges: voter apathy, electoral fraud, corruption. Citizens strengthen democracy by voting, obeying laws, participating in governance, and holding leaders accountable.
summary: Constitutional democracy = government limited by constitution. Features: separation of powers, federalism, fundamental rights, elections, rule of law.
nigerian_examples: 1999 Constitution
National Assembly checks Executive
INEC conducting elections

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: Nigeria has a mixed economy combining private enterprise and government control. Economic systems: capitalism (private ownership, profit motive, competition), socialism (government ownership, equality focus), mixed (both). Nigerian economy sectors: primary (agriculture, oil, mining - extraction), secondary (manufacturing, processing), tertiary (services, banking, telecom). Key institutions: Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) controls money supply, interest rates; Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE) for company shares. Economic challenges: over-reliance on oil, unemployment, inflation, infrastructure deficits. Economic opportunities: agriculture, technology, manufacturing, creative industries (Nollywood, music). Understanding economics helps citizens make financial decisions and hold government accountable.
summary: Nigeria has mixed economy (private + government). Sectors: primary (oil), secondary (manufacturing), tertiary (services). CBN controls money.
nigerian_examples: CBN sets interest rates
Dangote Group (private manufacturing)
Government-owned refineries
Nollywood generates revenue

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: Foreign policy is how Nigeria interacts with other countries. Key principles: African-centered (support for African unity, decolonization, anti-apartheid), non-alignment (not choosing superpower sides during Cold War), peaceful conflict resolution (diplomacy, not war), economic cooperation, respect for international law, protection of citizens abroad. Nigerian foreign policy under ECOWAS (Economic Community of West African States) promotes regional stability. Nigeria has contributed troops to UN peacekeeping missions (Liberia, Sierra Leone, Sudan, Somalia). Foreign policy achievements: ending apartheid in South Africa, leading ECOWAS peacekeeping, hosting African Union summits. Challenges: balancing relationships with China, US, UK; protecting Nigerians in diaspora; fighting terrorism with international partners.
summary: Foreign policy = Nigeria's relations with other countries. Principles: African-centered, peaceful conflict resolution, economic cooperation. ECOWAS, UN peacekeeping.
nigerian_examples: ECOWAS headquarters in Abuja
Nigerian troops in Liberia
Diplomatic relations with 190+ countries
President chairs AU summits

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: Human rights are basic freedoms and protections every person deserves regardless of nationality, religion, gender, or status. Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) outlines 30 rights. Key rights: right to life, liberty, security; freedom from slavery, torture; right to fair trial; freedom of expression, religion, assembly; right to education, work, healthcare. In Nigeria, Chapter IV of Constitution guarantees fundamental rights. Rights limitations: rights can be limited for public safety, national security, or others' rights. Rights violations in Nigeria: police brutality, extrajudicial killings, child abuse, discrimination. Defend rights by: speaking against injustice, reporting violations, supporting human rights organizations.
summary: Human rights = basic freedoms for all. Universal Declaration (1948). Nigerian Constitution Chapter IV guarantees rights. Defend rights by speaking against injustice.
nigerian_examples: Right to education for all children
Freedom of religion (Christianity, Islam, traditional)
Freedom of press (newspapers reporting)
Voting rights at 18

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: Sustainable development meets present needs without harming future generations. Three pillars: economic (growth, jobs, fair wages), social (education, healthcare, equality), environmental (protecting nature, reducing pollution). UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) - 17 goals for 2030 including: no poverty, zero hunger, quality education, clean water, affordable clean energy, climate action. Nigeria's challenges: poverty (40% live below poverty line), out-of-school children (10+ million), water pollution, deforestation, climate change impacts (flooding, desertification). Individual actions for sustainability: reduce waste (recycle, reuse), save water/electricity, plant trees, educate others, support green businesses. Nigeria's future depends on balancing growth with environmental care.
summary: Sustainable development = meet present needs without harming future. Three pillars: economic, social, environmental. UN SDGs 17 goals for 2030.
nigerian_examples: Recycling plastic bottles
Planting trees against desertification
Solar panels for electricity
Poverty reduction programs

subject: Teamwork
content: Cross-functional teams include members from different departments or skills working toward common goal. Example: launching new product needs marketing, design, engineering, finance. Benefits: diverse perspectives, faster problem-solving, innovation. Challenges: different priorities, communication barriers, turf wars. Success factors: clear shared goal, mutual respect, good facilitation, regular communication. Nigerian businesses use cross-functional teams for projects. In school, science projects need research, writing, art, presentation skills - each student contributes different strengths. Cross-functional experience valuable for future careers.
summary: Cross-functional teams have members from different skills/departments. Benefits: diverse perspectives, innovation. Challenges: different priorities. Success: clear goal, respect.
nigerian_examples: Product launch teams
School project groups
Event planning committees
Community development teams

subject: Teamwork
content: Performance metrics measure team effectiveness. Quantitative metrics: output (units produced, tasks completed), quality (defect rate, customer satisfaction), speed (cycle time, response time), efficiency (cost per unit). Qualitative metrics: communication effectiveness, collaboration, innovation, morale. Balanced scorecard approach: financial, customer, internal processes, learning/growth. Nigerian teams use metrics: school projects (grades, completion time), sports (points, assists), business (sales, profit, retention). For students: track assignments completed on time, group meeting attendance, peer feedback scores, learning outcomes. Metrics should be: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound. Use data to improve, not punish.
summary: Performance metrics measure team effectiveness. Quantitative: output, quality, speed, efficiency. Qualitative: communication, collaboration, morale. Balanced scorecard.
nigerian_examples: School project grades
Sports statistics
Business KPIs
Club attendance

subject: Teamwork
content: Team culture = shared values, beliefs, behaviors. Elements: psychological safety (safe to take risks, admit mistakes), accountability (members deliver commitments), clarity (roles, goals, processes), meaning (work matters), impact (results matter). Building positive culture: model desired behaviors, celebrate wins (big/small), address problems quickly, gather feedback, invest in relationships. Toxic culture signs: blame, secrets, cliques, fear, burnout. Nigerian examples: successful football teams (Super Eagles culture), business teams, school clubs. Students build team culture: inclusive language, share credit, help struggling teammates, resolve conflicts respectfully. Culture predicts performance - good culture helps good results, even with average talent.
summary: Team culture = shared values, beliefs, behaviors. Elements: psychological safety, accountability, clarity, meaning, impact. Build through modeling, celebrating, addressing problems.
nigerian_examples: Super Eagles culture
Business teams
School clubs
Community groups

subject: Teamwork
content: Team learning develops collective knowledge and capability. Processes: after-action reviews (what happened? what worked? what didn't? what will change?), retrospectives (regular reflection), knowledge sharing sessions, cross-training (learn each other's roles), learning from failures (blameless post-mortems). Benefits: avoids repeating mistakes, spreads best practices, builds shared mental models, increases adaptability. Nigerian examples: medical teams reviewing cases, engineering teams analyzing failures, sports teams watching game film. Student teams: debrief after projects, share study techniques, rotate roles. Learning teams outperform those that don't learn. Create psychological safety for honest reflection. Document lessons for future teams.
summary: Team learning develops collective knowledge. Processes: after-action reviews, retrospectives, knowledge sharing, cross-training, learning from failures. Avoids repeated mistakes.
nigerian_examples: Medical case reviews
Engineering failure analysis
Sports game film
Project debriefs

subject: Teamwork
content: Virtual teams work together online from different locations. Tools: Zoom, Slack, Google Docs, Trello, WhatsApp. Challenges: time zones, technology issues, less personal connection, miscommunication. Success strategies: clear communication (over-communicate), use video (builds trust), document decisions, set meeting times, respect time zones, use shared calendars, celebrate wins virtually. Nigerian students collaborate online for group projects using Google Docs and WhatsApp. Virtual teamwork skills are essential for future jobs. Practice: agree on communication tools, assign roles, meet regularly, update each other.
summary: Virtual teams work online from different locations. Tools: Zoom, Slack, Google Docs. Challenges: time zones, tech issues. Strategies: clear communication, video, documentation.

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: Advanced computer skills prepare you for secondary school. File organization: create folders, name files clearly, move files between folders. System settings: change background/wallpaper, adjust volume and brightness, set date and time. Using external devices: USB drives (save and open files), printers (print documents), scanners (copy pictures to computer). Keyboard shortcuts: Ctrl+C (copy), Ctrl+X (cut), Ctrl+V (paste), Ctrl+Z (undo), Ctrl+Y (redo), Ctrl+A (select all), Ctrl+F (find in document). Troubleshooting basics: restart computer for minor issues, check cables if something doesn't work, ask teacher for help. These skills help you succeed in secondary school computer classes.
summary: Advanced skills: file organization, system settings, external devices, keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Z), basic troubleshooting.

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: Digital citizenship means being responsible and safe online. Nine elements: digital access (everyone should have internet), digital commerce (buying/selling online legally), digital communication (respectful messaging), digital literacy (understanding technology), digital etiquette (manners online), digital law (no stealing, hacking, piracy), digital rights and responsibilities (privacy, free speech), digital health and wellness (balance screen time, posture), digital security (protecting information). Nigerian digital citizens: respect others online, don't share passwords, don't cyberbully, give credit for others' work, limit gaming/social media time, use strong passwords. Your online actions have real-world consequences.
summary: Digital citizenship = responsible online behavior. Nine elements: access, commerce, communication, literacy, etiquette, law, rights, health, security.
nigerian_examples: Respecting others in WhatsApp groups
Not downloading movies illegally
Limiting gaming time to focus on studies

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: Email is electronic mail used to send messages online. Parts of an email: To (recipient's address), Cc (carbon copy - sends copies to others), Subject (topic of message), Body (your message), Attachments (files like pictures or documents). Email etiquette: use a clear subject line, start with a greeting (Dear Mr. Ade), write clearly and politely, end with closing (Sincerely, Best regards). Never type in ALL CAPS (it looks like shouting). Check spelling before sending. Do not share private information. Reply to messages within a reasonable time. Nigerian students use email to contact teachers, submit assignments, and communicate with family abroad.
summary: Email parts: To, Subject, Body, Attachments. Etiquette: clear subject, greeting, polite language, closing, check spelling. No ALL CAPS.
nigerian_examples: Sending homework to teacher
Emailing a relative in another country
Applying for a school program

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides) creates slideshows for reports and speeches. Slide layout: title slide (topic and name), content slides (information), conclusion slide (summary). Design tips: use clear fonts (Arial, Calibri), limit text per slide (6 lines max), use bullet points not paragraphs, add relevant pictures. Transitions: effects between slides (use sparingly). Animations: effects on individual items (don't overdo). Presenting tips: practice before, speak clearly, look at audience not screen, don't read slides word-for-word. Nigerian students use presentations for class projects, cultural day reports, and school competitions.
summary: Presentation software creates slideshows. Design tips: clear fonts, limit text, use pictures. Practice before presenting, speak clearly, look at audience.
nigerian_examples: Presenting a report on Nigerian independence

Creating a presentation about Nigerian culture

subject: Basic Digital Literacy
content: A spreadsheet organizes data in rows and columns. Cells are individual boxes where you enter information. Rows are numbered (1,2,3). Columns have letters (A,B,C). Cell address combines column and row (A1, B2). Enter data: text, numbers, dates. Basic formulas start with = sign: =A1+B1 adds two cells, =SUM(A1:A10) adds a range. Simple formatting: bold headers, borders, colors. Creating a chart: select data, click Chart, choose bar or line chart. Spreadsheets help with budgets, grades, and lists. Nigerian students use spreadsheets for tracking expenses, project data, and simple calculations.
summary: Spreadsheets organize data in rows and columns. Cells have addresses (A1). Formulas start with = ( =A1+B1 ). Create charts from data.
nigerian_examples: Tracking pocket money expenses
Recording exam scores for multiple subjects
Creating a class attendance list

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Disease transmission is how illnesses spread. Direct contact: touching infected person (COVID-19, flu). Indirect contact: touching contaminated surfaces (doorknobs, phones). Airborne: breathing droplets from coughs/sneezes (tuberculosis, measles). Vector-borne: through mosquitoes (malaria), ticks (Lyme disease), rats (Lassa fever). Waterborne: drinking contaminated water (cholera, typhoid). Foodborne: eating contaminated food (salmonella). Prevention: wash hands, cover cough, clean surfaces, use mosquito nets, boil water, cook food thoroughly, get vaccinated. Nigerian diseases: malaria (leading cause of death), Lassa fever, cholera outbreaks, COVID-19. Understanding transmission helps you protect yourself and others.
summary: Disease transmission: direct contact, indirect contact, airborne, vector-borne, waterborne, foodborne. Prevention: handwashing, mosquito nets, clean water, vaccines.
nigerian_examples: Malaria prevention with bed nets
Cholera outbreaks during rainy season
COVID-19 handwashing campaigns
Lassa fever awareness in rural areas

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Ecology studies how living things interact with each other and their environment. An ecosystem includes all living (biotic: plants, animals, bacteria) and non-living (abiotic: water, soil, air, sunlight) components. Food chains show energy flow: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle. Food webs are interconnected food chains. Energy pyramids show decreasing energy at each level. Biomes: forest, grassland, desert, aquatic. Nigerian ecosystems: rainforest (south), savanna (middle), Sahel (north), mangrove (Niger Delta). Humans impact ecosystems through pollution, deforestation, and climate change. Conservation protects ecosystems for future generations.
summary: Ecology studies living/non-living interactions. Ecosystems have biotic and abiotic parts. Food chains show energy flow. Nigerian ecosystems: rainforest, savanna, Sahel, mangrove.
nigerian_examples: Rainforest in Cross River State
Savanna grassland in Kaduna
Mangrove forest in Niger Delta
Yankari National Park wildlife

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Environmental conservation protects natural resources for future generations. Renewable resources: forests, water, wind, solar (can replenish). Non-renewable resources: oil, coal, minerals (cannot replenish). Conservation methods: reduce waste, reuse items, recycle materials, plant trees, save water, use renewable energy. Nigerian conservation efforts: National Parks (Yankari, Gashaka-Gumti), afforestation programs (planting trees in Sahel), anti-deforestation laws, wildlife protection (endangered species). Individual actions: turn off lights, take short showers, use both sides of paper, pick up litter, plant a tree. Conservation saves money and protects the planet.
summary: Conservation protects natural resources. Renewable (trees, water) vs non-renewable (oil, coal). Reduce, reuse, recycle. Nigerian parks and laws.
nigerian_examples: Yankari National Park protecting wildlife
Tree planting campaigns in northern Nigeria
Recycling programs in Lagos
Ban on single-use plastics in some states

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: Nervous system controls body functions and responses. Central nervous system (brain, spinal cord). Peripheral nerves connect to rest of body. Neurons are nerve cells. Brain parts: cerebrum (thinking, memory, senses), cerebellum (balance, coordination), brainstem (breathing, heartbeat). Reflex arc (automatic response like pulling hand from hot). Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers. Nervous system health: sleep, nutrition (omega-3s), exercise, avoid alcohol/drugs, protect from injury (helmets). Nigerian neurology research advances.
summary: Nervous system controls body. CNS: brain, spinal cord. Brain parts: cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem. Neurons, reflexes, neurotransmitters.
nigerian_examples: Helmet safety campaigns
Neurology research centers
Brain injury prevention

subject: Basic Science & Technology
content: The reproductive system enables reproduction (creating offspring). Male reproductive system: testes (produce sperm), penis, sperm ducts. Female reproductive system: ovaries (produce eggs), fallopian tubes, uterus (where baby grows), vagina. Fertilization occurs when sperm meets egg in fallopian tube. The fertilized egg implants in uterus and grows into a baby over 9 months (pregnancy). Puberty is when reproductive system matures (ages 9-14 for girls, 10-15 for boys). Changes include body growth, hair growth, menstruation (girls), voice deepening (boys). Understanding reproduction helps young people make informed health decisions.
summary: Reproductive system enables reproduction. Male: testes, penis. Female: ovaries, uterus. Fertilization creates baby. Puberty matures system.
learning_objectives: Identify male and female reproductive organs
nigerian_examples: Puberty education in Nigerian schools
Family planning discussions
Menstrual hygiene management

subject: Communication
content: Listening comprehension is understanding spoken information accurately. Types of listening: Discriminative (distinguishing sounds), Informational (understanding facts), Critical (evaluating arguments), Empathetic (understanding feelings). Strategies: Focus attention (eliminate distractions), Predict content (anticipate what you'll hear), Identify main ideas, Take notes (key words, not everything), Ask clarifying questions, Summarize what you heard. Active listening body language: eye contact, nod, lean forward, don't interrupt. Nigerian students use listening comprehension in lectures, instructions, news, and conversations. Good listening improves grades, relationships, and job performance.
summary: Listening comprehension = understanding spoken information. Types: discriminative, informational, critical, empathetic. Strategies: focus, predict, identify main ideas, take notes, summarize.
nigerian_examples: Understanding teacher instructions
Following news reports on NTA
Comprehending sermons in church or mosque

subject: Communication
content: Media literacy is ability to access, analyze, evaluate, and create media. Types of media: news, social media, advertising, entertainment, educational. Critical questions: Who created this message? Why? Who is the target audience? What techniques attract attention? What values are represented? What is omitted? How might different people interpret this? Media literacy helps you: distinguish facts from opinions, recognize bias and propaganda, identify fake news, understand advertising persuasion, avoid misinformation. Nigerian media landscape: NTA, Channels TV, Arise TV, Punch newspaper, Premium Times, social media (WhatsApp, Twitter, Facebook, TikTok). Always verify information with multiple sources before sharing.
summary: Media literacy = analyze and evaluate media. Ask who created, why, target audience, techniques, values, omissions. Distinguish facts from opinions. Verify with multiple sources.
nigerian_examples: Comparing news reports from different Nigerian stations
Fact-checking viral WhatsApp messages
Analyzing political advertisements during elections

subject: Communication
content: Negotiation is discussing to reach agreement when people have different interests. Steps: Prepare (know your goal, know their likely goal, find common ground), Discuss (state your position clearly, listen to theirs), Propose (suggest solutions), Bargain (give and take, compromise), Agree (confirm understanding, shake hands). Principles: Separate people from problem (don't attack person), Focus on interests not positions (why they want what they want), Invent options for mutual gain (creative solutions), Use objective criteria (fair standards). In Nigerian culture, negotiation is common in markets (buying and selling), family decisions, and business. Win-win is best (both satisfied), not win-lose (one winner).
summary: Negotiation: discuss to reach agreement. Steps: prepare, discuss, propose, bargain, agree. Separate people from problem, focus on interests, invent options, use objective criteria.
learning_objectives: Apply to school and home situations
nigerian_examples: Bargaining at Onitsha market
Deciding whose turn to use computer
Splitting chores with siblings

subject: Communication
content: Public speaking mastery means delivering speeches with confidence and impact. Key elements: Preparation (research topic, know audience, organize content), Practice (rehearse aloud, time yourself, get feedback), Delivery (speak clearly, use pauses, vary tone, make eye contact), Body language (stand tall, use gestures, don't fidget), Handling nerves (breathe deeply, visualize success, start strong). Speech structure: Opening (hook attention: question, story, fact), Body (3 main points with evidence), Conclusion (summarize, call to action). Nigerian students practice public speaking in debates, assemblies, and competitions. Famous Nigerian speakers: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Chimamanda Adichie, Wole Soyinka.
summary: Public speaking mastery: preparation, practice, delivery, body language, handling nerves. Structure: opening, body, conclusion. Nigerian speakers: Adichie, Soyinka.

Inter-house debate competitions
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala's WTO speeches

subject: Communication
content: Strategic communication aligns messaging with organizational goals.
